title: New Survey Shows Rising Food Insecurity in Illinois
summary: New Survey Shows Rising Food Insecurity in Illinois Jessica Watts Wed, 11/25/2026 - 18:06 As millions of people prepare to celebrate Thanksgiving, a new survey is shining a light on food insecurity. Hunger Free America , a national nonprofit dedicated to ending domestic hunger, reported that 45% of Illinois residents are not always able to afford enough food. This growing rate follows a series of federal changes to SNAP requirements and cuts to grants that serve the country’s most in-need families. Participation in the federal food assistance program is at its lowest level since 2009, according to new data from the Illinois Department of Human Services. Food insecurity has more than tripled in the last two years, according to Amy Dolan, Chicago food action board coordinator at Hunger Free America. “People, unfortunately, have always been hungry across our state and our nation, and due to federal cuts and rising costs, we’ve only seen that increase greatly,” Dolan said. The Friendship Center, a food pantry on Chicago’s Northwest Side, offers grocery distribution four times per week, along with grocery delivery and a hot meal program. Nadia Jiménez, the center’s executive director, said she has seen more people than ever utilizing these services as many Chicagoans on the city’s South and West sides have turned to food pantries, soup kitchens and other free meal programs to fill the hole left by seven Save A Lot store closures this year. “People are coming (from) far and wide,” Jiménez said. “We’re very intentional of doing things like dignified care and making it feel like a grocery store and having things so we can address all the cultures that are surrounded in our neighborhood.” Though resources like the Friendship Center can help families with children meet basic needs, parents still struggle to find nutritious meals and meet sufficient portion sizes, according to Jiménez. Nonprofit leaders like Dolan and Jiménez have reported that food insecure families are often met with difficult choices on how to spend their money every day. “It’s unbelievable that a household would have to choose between feeding their children, or paying their rent or continuing to take care of their pet,” Dolan said. “It’s just evil, it’s unheard of. And it’s not something that we’re about in Illinois and that we want to be about in Illinois. When we think about taking care of our neighbors and taking care of each other, I want to believe this is not who we are.” The recent midterm election focused overwhelmingly on affordability, as the cost of groceries, gas and housing were top of mind for millions of Americans. As Democrats made historic wins across the country, Jiménez said change is needed at a federal, state and local level to see lasting impacts. “It’s very invigorating to see the blue wave that came through, and of course everyone is very excited,” Jiménez said. “We’ve got things to change and they have to change now. … That foot on the gas pedal can’t be let go. And I think that’s why and how we got to where we are right now.” Health
